excerpt_original: Born in Mexico City in 1942, Graciela Iturbide became Manuel Álvarez Bravo’s assistant before building, from the 1970s on, one of the most intuitive bodies of work in Latin American photography, from the Zapotec women of Juchitán to the Seri people of the Sonoran desert……

blocks.text: Born in Mexico City in 1942, Graciela Iturbide studied film before becoming the assistant of Manuel Álvarez Bravo, who taught her to look. Since the 1970s she has photographed her country with an intuitive, patient eye, from the Zapotec community of Juchitán, where women run the market, to the Seri people of the Sonoran desert, and to the birds that recur throughout her work. Always in black and white, her images blur the line between documentary and ritual. She received the W. Eugene Smith Grant in 1987 and the Hasselblad Award in 2008.

This segment comes from “Investigation,” the first episode of the seventh season of Art21’s documentary series “Art in the Twenty-First Century,” which premiered on PBS in October 2014. Iturbide describes a practice built on intuition and surprise, and the film follows her through “Frida’s Bathroom” (2005–06), the series she made in the bathroom of Frida Kahlo’s house in Mexico City.
17 minutes, in Spanish with English subtitles.
